My handkerchief, you understand, was inside my helmet, along with a few other articles; but this happened to be a helmet a man couldn't remove without assistance. That hadn't entered my head when I stowed it there; indeed, I hadn't known it. I had imagined it would be wonderfully convenient. Now the knowledge that it lay so close, practically at hand and yet impossible to reach, made the whole business harder to endure. Yes, what you can't lay hands on is generally what you most want; everybody has observed that. Well, it drove everything else from my thoughts, swept them clean away and fixed them inside my helmet. Mile after mile they remained there, imagining that handkerchief, conjuring up that handkerchief. It was maddening to feel the salty perspiration trickle into my eyes while I couldn't reach it. In print this may seem a trifling inconvenience, but it was nothing of the sort; it was misery of the most substantial kind. I wouldn't claim that unless it were true. I resolved to bring a reticule next time, regardless of its appearance or anybody's remarks. Naturally, those iron-clad dandies of the Round Table would call it disgraceful and perhaps raise Sheol over it, but I wanted comfort first and fashion second. We jogged onward, occasionally coming upon a dusty stretch where clouds rose about us, filling my nose and making me sneeze and weep. Of course I said things better left unsaid; I don't pretend otherwise. I'm no better than other people.

In this solitary Britain we seemed unable to encounter a soul, not even an ogre. Considering my temper just then, that was fortunate for the ogre—an ogre carrying a handkerchief, I mean. Most knights would have cared only about taking his armor. As far as I was concerned, he might keep his ironmongery, provided I secured his bandanna.

All the while it grew steadily hotter inside. The sun, you see, kept beating upon the iron and heating it further. When you're hot in that fashion, every small thing gets on your nerves. At a trot I clattered like a box of crockery, which irritated me; besides, I could scarcely bear the shield swinging and banging first against my chest, then around my back. If I slowed to a walk, my joints squealed and creaked with the tiresome sound of a wheelbarrow. At that pace we stirred up no breeze, so I was in danger of being fried inside that stove. Worse still, the more quietly we moved, the heavier the iron pressed upon me, and with every passing minute I seemed to weigh several additional tons.

Receive me, spirits of the tempest! Powers of destruction, stretch wide your arms and embrace me for ever—unless a gentler power has ordained some other fate, permitting me, after enduring long, to win my recompense and once more feel my heart beating close to the heart of a fellow creature.

At my feet lay Tiber, the highway traced by nature's own hand across her continent, with many boats fastened along its banks. Into one of these I would step with a handful of books, provisions, and my dog, and drift upon the river's current to the sea. Then, remaining near the land, I would follow the lovely coast and sun-bright promontories of the blue Mediterranean, pass Naples and the shores of Calabria, and venture through the double danger of Scylla and Charybdis. Thereafter, with undaunted purpose—for what remained for me to lose?—I would glide over the ocean toward Malta and the farther Cyclades. Constantinople I would shun; the sight of its familiar towers and inlets belonged to an existence unlike my present one. I would skirt Asia Minor and Syria and, beyond the seven-mouthed Nile, turn north once more, until forgotten Carthage and forsaken Libya vanished behind me and I gained the pillars of Hercules. And afterward—where mattered nothing—the ocean's oozy caverns and silent depths might house me before that protracted journey ended. The shaft of disease might pierce my heart as I floated alone upon the tossing Mediterranean; or at some port of call I might discover the thing I sought—a companion. Failing this, throughout unending time, decrepit and grey, my youth already entombed with my loved ones, the solitary voyager would continue to spread his sail and grasp the tiller. Obedient still to the winds of heaven, he would round promontory after promontory for ever, anchor in one bay and then another, and still furrow the unfruitful ocean. Leaving my native Europe's green lands behind, descending Africa's tawny coastline and weathering the savage seas about the Cape, I might secure my battered skiff in a creek beneath spice-bearing groves, among the fragrant islands of the remote Indian Ocean.

Wild dreams indeed. Yet from the moment they visited me a week ago, as I stood upon the summit of St. Peter's, they have governed my imagination. My boat is chosen, my slender provisions gathered. I have picked a few books, chiefly Homer and Shakespeare; but all the world's libraries lie open to me, and at any harbour I may replenish my supply. I entertain no hope that things will improve; yet this unvarying present has become unbearable.

He slipped furtively from the wooden panelling, a wicked smile upon his cruel, creased lips. As he crept past the great oriel window, where his arms and those of his murdered wife shone in blue and gold, the moon concealed her face behind a cloud. He drifted onward like a malignant shadow, and the darkness itself appeared to recoil from his passing. Once, fancying he heard a call, he halted; but the sound was merely a dog baying at the Red Farm. He resumed his course, muttering peculiar sixteenth-century oaths and occasionally flourishing his rusty dagger through the midnight air. At length he came to the corner of the corridor leading to unfortunate Washington's chamber. He lingered there a moment while the wind tossed his long grey hair and twisted the unspeakable horror of his burial shroud into strange, grotesque folds. Then the quarter-hour sounded from the clock, and he knew his moment had arrived. Chuckling inwardly, he rounded the corner. Instantly he recoiled with a miserable cry of fright and buried his whitened face in his long, skeletal hands. Directly before him stood a dreadful apparition, still as a carved statue and hideous as a lunatic's dream! Its head was smooth and shining; its face broad, plump, and white. Horrible laughter seemed to have contorted its features into a perpetual grin. Scarlet beams poured from its eyes, and its open mouth was a deep pit of flame. An appalling robe resembling his own wrapped the enormous figure in noiseless snow. Upon its chest hung a notice inscribed in strange, ancient lettering, apparently some register of disgrace, some chronicle of monstrous sins, some dreadful catalogue of crimes. Its right hand held high a curved sword of glittering steel.

Since he had never encountered a ghost before, he was naturally exceedingly alarmed. After casting another hurried look at the frightful figure, he fled to his room, stumbling over his long shroud as he raced down the passage. In the end he dropped the rusty dagger into the Minister's jackboots, where the butler discovered it next morning. Safe in the seclusion of his chamber, he threw himself onto a little pallet and thrust his face beneath the bedclothes. Presently, however, the courage of the old Canterville spirit returned, and he resolved to speak with the other ghost once daylight came. Accordingly, as the first dawn silvered the hills, he went back toward the place where he had first beheld that ghastly presence. After all, he reflected, two ghosts were preferable to one, and with his new friend's assistance he might tackle the twins without danger.
